519.title: Manthara
519.hook: a battlefield promise the king forgot, and a maid who remembered
519.carry: the rest will be done by a promise
519.howItsDone: The kopa-griha, or anger room, appears in this episode of the Ayodhya Kanda; storytellers often pause here to point out how Manthara builds her plan from the king's love and his pride in keeping his word.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Manthara painted a future where Bharata is lost, and Kaikeyi, after pushing back, asked how to stop it. Today, an old promise. A new week begins.

Years before Rama was born, the gods went to war with a demon named Shambara and asked King Dasharatha to fight beside them. Kaikeyi rode with him. The king was badly wounded and fell unconscious, and Kaikeyi drove his chariot out of the fighting and saved his life. When he woke, he said: ask me for two things, anything. I'll ask later, she said. And then, it seems, she forgot. Manthara didn't.
screen: `A WAR WITH SHAMBARA.` → `KAIKEYI SAVES THE KING.` → `ASK ME FOR TWO THINGS.`

segments.voice: Kaikeyi asks how to stop the coronation, and Manthara answers with Kaikeyi's own story. Don't you remember? You told it to me yourself. The king owes you two boons. Ask now. First, that Bharata be consecrated as heir. Second, that Rama be sent to the Dandaka forest for fourteen years, living as an ascetic: long enough, Manthara reasons, for Bharata to win the people's hearts and put down roots. Then the plan, step by step. Go to the anger room, where a wronged queen goes. Take off your jewels, put on soiled clothes, lie on the bare floor. When the king comes, don't look at him, don't speak. He can't bear to see you upset. He'll offer gems and gold; refuse them. Make him swear first, and only then ask. It's unsettling because it's so practical. Manthara knows the king's heart better than he does: his love for Kaikeyi, and his pride in keeping his word. She builds the trap out of those two good things. Kaikeyi, fully won, praises her warmly and promises her gold ornaments when Bharata rules. Then she does exactly as she's told: into the anger room, jewelry scattered on the floor, and down onto the bare floor. Manthara's part is done. The rest will be done by a promise.

520.title: Kaikeyi's boons
520.hook: the king swears by the one person he can't live without, and that's the trap closing
520.carry: a gift the receiver gets to choose
520.howItsDone: In the epic, a vara, a boon, once granted binds the one who gave it, and this scene shows a king's pride in his word becoming the thing that holds him.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Manthara, and the king's forgotten battlefield promise. Kaikeyi lay down on the floor of the anger room. Today, the king walks in.

Dasharatha has had a wonderful day. The assembly said yes, the city is glowing, and tomorrow his favorite son becomes his heir. He wants to tell the person he most enjoys telling things to, so he walks to Kaikeyi's rooms, which Valmiki describes as beautiful, full of birds and music and flowering trees. Her couch is empty. A doorkeeper tells him, nervously, that the queen has gone into the anger room. And the king, happy a moment ago, goes cold.
screen: `A WONDERFUL DAY.` → `HER COUCH IS EMPTY.` → `SHE'S IN THE ANGER ROOM.`

segments.voice: He finds her on the floor among her scattered jewels, kneels, and strokes her hair. Are you ill? Has someone insulted you? Tell me who, and I'll punish them; tell me who you want rewarded, and I'll reward them. Anything you want is yours. It's exactly the opening Manthara predicted. Kaikeyi asks him to swear first. And Dasharatha, wanting only to see her get up off the floor, swears by the one he loves most. There's no one I love more than you, he says, except Rama, without whom I couldn't live an hour. By Rama, I'll do what you ask. Now Kaikeyi makes the promise as public as she can. She calls the gods to witness: sun and moon, sky and planets, night and day, the directions, the earth, the beings of the heavens and the household gods. Let them all hear that the king has sworn. She reminds him of the war with Shambara, the day she saved his life, and the two boons. And she asks. Let Bharata be consecrated with the waters that are ready. Let Rama go to the Dandaka forest for fourteen years, in bark and deerskin, with matted hair. The Sanskrit for boon is vara, a gift the receiver gets to choose. These two were freely given, years ago, out of gratitude. Tonight they come due, and the king learns what he gave away.

521.title: Kaikeyi's boons
521.hook: a king spends the whole night arguing with his own promise
521.howItsDone: In the Ramayana, satya, truthfulness, is the king's proudest virtue, and this night is its hard case: a true word that brings grief.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kaikeyi's boons, claimed. The king swore by Rama before he heard them: Bharata crowned, Rama to the forest. Today, the longest night in Ayodhya.

Deep in the night, in Kaikeyi's room, the king of Ayodhya, who commands armies, is on the floor beside his queen, trying to find a way out of something he swore a few hours ago. He tries one door, then another, then the first again. Valmiki doesn't hurry this night. He lets it run, speech after speech, the way a sleepless night runs. And through all of it, Kaikeyi gives one answer.
screen: `DEEP IN THE NIGHT.` → `THE KING, ON THE FLOOR.` → `ONE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Hearing the boons, the king faints. When he comes to, he tries everything. He pleads: what has Rama done to you? You've praised him yourself; he honors you like his own mother. He reasons: the people will call me a fool, a king ruled by a woman. Kausalya will be shattered. And Bharata himself will never accept a throne taken this way. He rages, and says terrible things. Then he falls at her feet and begs. Kaikeyi doesn't move, and her answer is more than stubbornness. She argues from the thing he's proudest of, his truthfulness. You gave your word, she says, with the gods as witnesses. She names old kings famous for keeping promises at any cost: Shibi, who gave his own flesh to a hawk to save a dove that came to him for shelter, and Alarka, who gave away his eyes when a brahmin asked. Break your word, and you'll be the king who broke his word. Here is the knot at the center of the Ayodhya Kanda. The word is satya, truth, and it means more than not lying: your word holding, as good as a thing done. Dasharatha has built his life on satya, and now it's turned against the son he loves. He can't break his promise without breaking himself, or keep it without breaking Rama. The text says he begged the night itself not to end. But morning comes.
screen: `THE KING PLEADS, REASONS, RAGES.` · `KAIKEYI ANSWERS: YOU GAVE YOUR WORD.` · `SHIBI AND THE DOVE, ALARKA'S EYES.` · `SATYA: A WORD THAT HOLDS.` · then, large: `BUT MORNING COMES.`

522.title: Kaikeyi's boons
522.hook: Rama rides to his coronation through cheering streets, and finds his father unable to speak
522.carry: the king says one word: Rama
522.howItsDone: In the text, Rama's phrase that he does not say things twice comes before he knows what he has agreed to; it is a picture of a person whose word is final.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the longest night. The king begged, and Kaikeyi held him to satya, a word that holds. Today, morning comes.

Outside the palace, nobody knows. The sun rises on the morning Ayodhya has prepared for. Vasishtha arrives with his students and the sacred waters. The streets are full. Bards sing outside the king's door to wake him, as they do every morning. Inside, the king hasn't slept, and he can't stand up. Two worlds, one wall, and in a moment Rama will walk from one into the other.
screen: `OUTSIDE, NOBODY KNOWS.` → `BARDS SING AT THE KING'S DOOR.` → `TWO WORLDS, ONE WALL.`

segments.voice: The charioteer Sumantra goes in to say everything is ready. The king can barely speak. Kaikeyi answers for him: bring Rama here. Sumantra, puzzled, goes. Rama rides through packed streets and hears the people as he passes: today he'll be made heir; how fortunate we are. Women lean from windows to see him. In Kaikeyi's room he finds his father on a couch, pale, beside the queen. Rama bows to his father's feet, then to Kaikeyi's. The king manages one word, Rama, and then his eyes fill and he can't say more. Rama has never seen his father like this. Frightened, he turns to Kaikeyi. Have I done something wrong? Is he ill? Has someone hurt him? The king won't speak, she says, because he's afraid to tell you something unpleasant. He made me a promise. If you'll do what he promised, I'll tell you. And Rama, not knowing what's coming, says something he can't take back. At my father's word I would walk into fire. I would drink poison. Tell me what he wants. I promise to do it, and Rama doesn't say things twice. So Kaikeyi tells him, plainly. Bharata consecrated with the waters made ready for Rama. Rama to the Dandaka forest for fourteen years, in bark clothes, with matted hair. Notice who says it. Not the king, who lies there unable to speak. The boons arrive in Kaikeyi's voice, to a son who has just promised to obey.

523.title: Rama's calm
523.hook: he loses a kingdom in one sentence, and the first thing he asks about is his father
523.howItsDone: Later devotional tradition calls Rama maryada purushottama, the ideal of right conduct, and this scene, his calm acceptance of exile, shows what that title means.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kaikeyi's boons, delivered. The king could say only one word, Rama, so Kaikeyi told Rama herself. Today, Rama answers.

The consecration waters stand in gold vessels outside the door. The priests are ready. The city is singing. And inside Kaikeyi's room, the man it was all for has just heard that none of it is his: not today, not for fourteen years. He's to go to the forest, in bark clothes. A person could shout here, or plead, or ask whose idea this was. Rama has every right to. Listen to what he says instead.
screen: `THE WATERS ARE WAITING.` → `NONE OF IT IS HIS.` → `WHAT DOES HE SAY?`

segments.voice: Rama hears Kaikeyi out, and the text says he isn't pained. He answers simply. So be it. I'll go to the forest, in bark and matted hair, to keep the king's promise. Then the one thing that does hurt: why didn't my father tell me himself? He didn't need to grieve over this. I'd give Bharata the kingdom gladly, and Sita, and my life, if my father asked. Send messengers to bring Bharata home. Kaikeyi, relieved, pushes once more: go today; your father won't eat or bathe until you've left. Rama doesn't flare. Don't take me for someone who lives for wealth, he says, in effect. Know me as one who lives like the sages, by dharma. Then he goes, and Valmiki gives us a detail to keep. Passing the gold vessels and the consecration waters, Rama walks around them respectfully, honoring something sacred that's no longer meant for him. He turns away the royal umbrella and the fans. He keeps his voice level, so the people waiting outside won't be frightened. Losing the kingdom took nothing from his radiance, Valmiki says, the way night takes nothing from the beauty of the moon. Is this calm the same as not feeling? The text doesn't say so. Later in this very book Rama grieves, and later still he'll weep openly. Today's calm is a choice: in the moment of loss, he protects his father's word, his brother's honor, and the people outside the door.

524.title: Rama's calm
524.hook: his mother is praying for his coronation when he walks in to tell her
524.howItsDone: Tying a protective thread on someone's wrist before a journey or a rite is still common in Hindu families; in the text, Kausalya blesses Rama at length and ties one on his arm before he leaves.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama's calm. So be it, he said, and honored the vessels meant for him. Today, the hardest conversation: his mother.

Kausalya has been up since before dawn, dressed in white silk by the sacred fire, making offerings for her son's success. She's waited years for this morning. Valmiki tells us she's long been the least favored of the king's wives, and today was going to change that. Then Rama comes in. She's so glad to see him she rises to bless him, and offers him a seat and something to eat. And he has to tell her.
screen: `KAUSALYA AT THE SACRED FIRE.` → `SHE'S WAITED YEARS.` → `AND HE HAS TO TELL HER.`

segments.voice: Rama tells her gently, and she collapses. When she can speak, her grief pours out. If I'd had no son at all, she says, I'd have had one sorrow. Now I have this. She's ready to follow him into the forest. Lakshmana is in the room too, furious; we'll come back to his anger in a few days. Today, watch Rama. He doesn't raise his voice, and he doesn't change his mind. He reminds her of others who obeyed a father's word at great cost, and one example is startling: Parashurama, the sage with the axe we met on the road, who once obeyed his father even against his own mother. Then Rama turns to Kausalya's own path. Your place is with the king, he says. He's old and grieving. Stay with him. Slowly she steadies, and the scene turns. Kausalya stops arguing and starts blessing. She calls on the gods, the seasons, the rivers, the mountains, the days and nights, to protect her son wherever he goes. Valmiki gives her blessing at length, and she ties a protective thread on his arm. Here's the thread back to the Ramayana's first verses, where Valmiki asks Narada: who in the world has mastered himself, ātmavān ko jitakrodho, who has conquered anger? Jitakrodha. Today we see what it looks like. Not a man without feelings, but a son who holds his mother's grief, his brother's rage and his own loss in one room, and stays kind.
screen: `KAUSALYA'S GRIEF POURS OUT.` · `RAMA ANSWERS WITH STEADINESS.` · `HER GRIEF TURNS TO BLESSING.` · `JITAKRODHA: ANGER CONQUERED.` · then, large: `HOLD EVERYTHING, AND STAY KIND.`

525.title: Rama's calm
525.hook: everyone in the palace wants someone to blame, and Rama won't
525.howItsDone: Sanskrit texts name two forces, daiva, fate or what the gods give, and purushakara, human effort; in the Ramayana the two sides are spoken by two brothers, Rama here and Lakshmana soon after.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama's calm with his mother, until her grief turned to blessing. Today, the question of blame, and the end of a week.

Who did this? In Ayodhya today, three answers are ready: Kaikeyi, Manthara, the king. Knowing who's responsible matters; it's how a wrong gets named and mended. But a hunt for blame can become its own fire, and burn longer than the thing that started it. Lakshmana is already reaching for the names. Rama is the one person with every right to say them out loud. And he refuses.
screen: `WHO DID THIS?` → `BLAME CAN BECOME ITS OWN FIRE.` → `RAMA REFUSES THE NAMES.`

segments.voice: Lakshmana is still burning, and Rama speaks to him directly. Put away the things gathered for the coronation, he says, and help me get ready to go. Then, surprisingly, he talks about Kaikeyi. Don't blame her. She has never treated me differently from her own son. If she has suddenly asked for this, cruel as it is, something larger than her is at work. His word is daiva, what comes from the gods, what we'd call fate or destiny. No one can fight what is given this way, he says. Happiness and sorrow, gain and loss, birth and death: they come, and nobody fully knows why. It could sound like giving up. But look at what it does in the story: it takes the hatred out of the room. Rama isn't saying Kaikeyi did nothing. He's refusing to make her the enemy, because she was once a mother to him and may be again. Lakshmana will argue the other side soon, and Valmiki will let him. Today, notice just this: Rama uses the idea to protect someone who has hurt him. And the week behind us: a maid's plan, an old promise claimed, a king's night of pleading, a father who could only say his son's name, and three days of Rama's calm. So be it to Kaikeyi, steadiness for his mother, and now, no blame for anyone.
screen: `PUT AWAY THE CORONATION THINGS.` · `DON'T BLAME KAIKEYI.` · `DAIVA: WHAT THE GODS GIVE.` · `TAKING THE HATRED OUT OF THE ROOM.` · then, large: `A WEEK: A PLAN, A PROMISE, A CALM.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you've been blaming, for something large or small, and picture their face. Without deciding they were right, try to see them as Rama saw Kaikeyi: someone once kind to you, who might be again. Breathe out, and loosen your grip on their name; you can pick it back up later if you need to.
